title: Field bits annotary and proposed shims — micro-prioritization
body:
Purpose:
Quick synthesis of recent field captures (Aug–Oct 2026) with lean, implementable micro-patches (we're calling them ‘shims’) that engineering can consider for near-term sprints. This doc is intentionally terse — think sketch + decision input rather than polished roadmap.

Context / how this was made:
- Source: 34 customer conversations (CS touchpoints), 12 incident threads, product support logs (latency/edgecases), and two paid pilot reports.
- Focus: production runtime pain that directly affects customer confidence (not feature wishlist).
- Method: cluster raw quotes into short problem statements, propose low-effort shims, and estimate likely customer impact and engineering cost (T-shirt).

Topline themes (short):
1) Visibility mismatch: customers want clearer signal when we fall back to a cheaper/compatible model variant. They notice content shifts and ask for explicit routing metadata in responses.
2) Small hallucination spikes tied to short context truncation in multi-turn flows (esp. system-message heavy dialogs).
3) Cost vs. quality nudges: customers want a simple per-endpoint knob to bias toward lower latency / lower cost without changing prompts.
4) Observability gaps: when retries happen or KV-cache misses are frequent, tooling often surfaces only 1–2 metrics; teams ask for traceable request-level flags to debug.
5) Onboarding friction: first 48 hours of traffic see surprising token burn due to large default generation lengths in example apps.

Representative customer verbatims (anonymized):
- "Our app suddenly answers differently and we couldn't tell whether it was a fallback — we lost a user because tone changed."
- "Intermittent hallucinations pop up only after long back-and-forth, seems like earlier context not being preserved."
- "We need a cheap toggle to trade 10% latency for 20–30% cost savings for low-priority flows."

Proposed micro-patches (shims) — prioritized for low cost, high clarity:
A — Response-level routing badge (very low effort, frontend/back compat).
  - What: Add a small field returned in the streaming response metadata: "model_variant_hint" (values: pinned | fallback | surrogate). When we switch to a compatible variant due to capacity/policy, the field is set.
  - Why: immediate customer visibility, reduces support churn.
  - Rough effort: 1 engineer, 3 days backend + 1 day SDK tweak + 1 day doc.
  - Likely impact: high WA (customer trust) — many pilot customers requested this.
  - Edge notes: keep off by default for compliance-sensitive customers; expose via per-API toggle.

B — Short-context leakage probe + guard (medium effort).
  - What: automated probe that replays recent n-turns against the active model configuration and flags potential early-truncation patterns; when flagged, return a diagnostic entry in the trace log (not exposed to end-user).
  - Why: helps SRE + CS pinpoint whether hallucinations correlate with cache evictions, truncated token windows, or system-message overflow.
  - Effort: 2 engineers, ~2 sprints to stabilise (probe + alert rules).
  - Impact: medium (reduces MTTR and engineering hours for root cause).

C — Endpoint-level cost/latency bias toggle (shim UX + routing rule)
  - What: a per-endpoint config (simple slider in Console + API flag) that biases routing to cheaper variants when latency budget is relaxed. Defaults: balanced.
  - Why: answers frequent ask from mid-market customers who want predictable economics without prompt surgery.
  - Effort: 1 eng (routing changes) + 1 product UX + document ~2 sprints.
  - Impact: high for Dedicated customers and cost-sensitive hosted users.

D — Request-level trace enrichment for KV-cache and retry events (low–medium).
  - What: enrich trace payloads to include cache_hit: true/false, kv_eviction_hint, and retry_reason for each request in Console traces.
  - Why: current traces show high latency but not whether cache misses caused it.
  - Effort: 1 engineer + 1 SRE, ~1 sprint.
  - Impact: high for debugging; also helps product detect workload patterns for Optimize recommendations.

E — Onboarding default length clamp (very low).
  - What: reduce example app generation default from 256 tokens to 64 in quickstarts and SDK examples; add a short explainer about token economics.
  - Why: immediate reduction in token burn for new signups and fewer surprise bills.
  - Effort: docs + examples update, <1 day.
  - Impact: low engineering cost, immediate customer goodwill.

Quick win bundle suggestions (release sprint 0 / quick patch):
- Implement A (routing badge) + E (default clamp) as a duo—fast to ship, high perception ROI.
- Add an internal blog/annotated example that calls out how to detect a fallback in logs (crosslink to Console).

Engineering asks / open implementation questions:
- For A: how to expose in streaming vs non-streaming payloads without breaking existing SDKs? (Options: new field in top-level response envelope + SDK patch).
- For B: do we run probes in prod synthetic runner or reuse sampling from customer traffic (privacy implications)? Need legal sign-off for any persisted diagnostic content.
- For C: routing bias could interact with SLA tiers — product and sales need to agree on defaults for each tier.

Risk/notes from SRE/product:
- Any exposed routing hints could leak internal capacity signals. Recommend per-account opt-in and obfuscation for hosted customers unless requested.
- Probe/diagnostic data must be gated for customers with strict data retention/PII rules.

Metrics / acceptance signals we can use to judge success:
- Customer support volume about "unexpected content change" down by 50% after A shipped (baseline tracked from Sep–Oct 2026).
- Token burn for first 7-day active users decreases >= 20% after E changes.
- Mean time to diagnose KV-cache-related hallucination events drops by 30% after D/B.

Suggested next steps (for this doc cycle):
1) Prioritise A + E for a quick patch sprint. Assign owners: Marcus for backend, Olga for SDK/docs.
2) Kick off scoping for B and D in the next eng-plan meeting (add ENG-8891 to scope).
3) Draft a short customer note template announcing the routing badge pilot (Samir to draft).
4) Check legal on diagnostic retention for probe logs (CS to escalate).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add a small appendix with sample payloads for A (stream + non-stream) and a one-line note about backwards compatibility.
- Run a 2-week pilot with 3 customers (we have 4 interested pilots flagged in Jira CS-4127).

Appendix (sketch):
- Example non-stream payload snippet (minimal): {response_text: "...", model_variant_hint: "fallback"} — include as an opt-in header.
- Example Console toggle: "Expose model variant hint" (off by default) with link to docs.

Unresolved questions to surface in next review:
- How should we label transient fallbacks vs permanent pinned variants in billing reports?
- Will third-party review (compliance) require the routing hint to be suppressed for some accounts?

End — quick, actionable, and designed to be developer-friendly. Ping me (Aisha) on Slack if you want me to turn any shim into a one-pager for product review.
